title: The Retention Trap: Why Churn Analysis Alone Won't Save Your Product
excerpt: Most teams treat retention like a math problem — measure churn, segment the lost users, and try to win them back. But retention isn't an analytics problem. It's a product thesis problem, and chasing churn numbers without understanding why people leave is how you end up optimizing the wrong thing.
content:
Here's a scenario that plays out at startups everywhere: your monthly churn ticks up from 4% to 6%, and suddenly retention is all anyone talks about. You dig into the data. You segment by cohort, by plan tier, by acquisition channel. You find that users who don't hit the "aha moment" in their first week are three times more likely to leave. So you ship an onboarding tooltip, a welcome email sequence, and a redesigned getting-started page.

Two months later, churn is still 6%. What went wrong?

You solved the signal, not the problem. And that's the retention trap: confusing what churn data tells you with what churn data means.

What Churn Data Actually Tells You

Churn is a lagging indicator. By the time someone cancels, they've been disengaged for weeks or months — they just finally made it official. Looking at churn numbers is like studying skid marks instead of learning to drive. You can describe the accident in perfect detail without understanding what caused it.

This matters because churn analysis is fundamentally descriptive. It tells you who left, when, and sometimes what they did before leaving. It does not tell you why they left, whether they're coming back, or what would have kept them. Those are causal questions, and descriptive data can't answer them.

The Three Fallacies of Churn-Driven Retention

1. The "Win Back" Fallacy

If you know which users churned, you can re-engage them with a discount, a feature announcement, or a "we miss you" email. This works — sometimes. But it treats retention as a marketing problem when it's usually a product problem. Users who leave because the product doesn't solve their problem will come back for a month on a discount and leave again when the discount expires. You haven't retained them; you've rented them.

2. The "Feature Gap" Fallacy

Churn analysis often reveals patterns like "users who don't use Feature X within 30 days churn at 2x the rate." The natural response is to drive adoption of Feature X. But correlation isn't causation. Feature X might be popular among users who were already committed, not the reason they stayed. Forcing engagement with a feature that doesn't fit the user's actual workflow just creates friction that drives more churn.

3. The "Segment and Solve" Fallacy

Breaking churn down by segment — enterprise vs. SMB, new vs. mature, demographic A vs. B — feels productive. Each segment gets a retention playbook. But segments are usually proxies for underlying problems you haven't identified yet. You're treating symptoms, notdiagnosis.

What Actually Works

Retention improves when you understand the job your product is hired to do and whether you're actually doing it well. That requires qualitative work: talking to churned users, watching how current users engage, and being honest about where the product falls short of the promise.

Start with three questions:

  • Why did you start using the product? — This reveals the job-to-be-done and whether you're delivering on it.
  • What would have made you stay? — This is the most direct retention insight you'll ever get, and it's almost never in your analytics dashboard.
  • What did you use instead before you found us? — This tells you about the competition and the baseline expectations you're competing against.

Then look at your active users and ask the flip side: what are they getting out of the product that they couldn't get elsewhere? That's your retention thesis. Everything else is optimization around a guess.

The Metric That Matters More Than Churn

Churn tells you how many people left. The more important metric is why the people who stayed, stayed. If you can't articulate the specific value that retains your best users — in their words, not your roadmap — then you don't have a retention strategy. You have a churn rate and a hope.

Retention isn't something you fix with a dashboard. It's something you build into the product from the start, by solving a real problem for a specific group of people better than the alternatives. Do that, and churn takes care of itself. Everything else is just rearranging deck chairs.

title: Customer Discovery: The Questions That Actually Matter
excerpt: Most customer interviews go wrong before the first question is asked. Teams show up with a script full of leading questions and leave with confirmation bias disguised as insight. The difference between a useless interview and a breakthrough one isn't the number of questions — it's the quality of what you choose not to ask.
content:
The Interview Nobody Needed

A PM schedules thirty minutes with a potential user. They open a doc with fourteen questions, all carefully worded to be "open-ended." They ask about pain points, current workflows, and what the user would want in a solution. The user answers thoughtfully. The PM leaves feeling like they learned something. Two weeks later, they build the feature the user described. It flops.

What happened? The user gave accurate answers to the wrong questions. They described their current behavior honestly, expressed mild interest in the proposed solution, and the PM mistook expressed interest for validated need. This is the most common failure mode in customer discovery, and it's entirely avoidable.

The Questions to Stop Asking

These questions feel productive but reliably produce garbage:

  • "Would you use a product that did X?" — People are polite. They will tell you yes to almost anything that sounds like it might help. This measures social agreeableness, not intent.
  • "How much would you pay for X?" — Pricing discovered through direct questioning is fiction. People have no reference point for a product that doesn't exist yet. Their guesses reflect their desire to be helpful, not their actual willingness to pay.
  • "What's your biggest pain point?" — Everyone has dozens. The question is too broad to surface the specific problem worth solving, and the answer is usually whatever pain is most top-of-mind today, not what they'd prioritize solving.
  • "What features would you want?" — This is how you end up building feature factories. Users are great at describing their problems in their own language and terrible at designing solutions. Ask about the problem, not the feature.

The Questions That Actually Work

The goal of a discovery interview is not to get someone to endorse your idea. It's to understand their behavior, their context, and the gap between what they currently do and what they need. The best questions are about the past and the present — never the future.

Past Behavior

  • "Walk me through the last time you encountered [problem area]." — Specificity forces honesty. It's harder to give a generic answer about a real event than to speculate about an abstract scenario.
  • "What did you do right before that? Right after?" — This maps the actual workflow and surfaces adjacent problems you didn't know existed.
  • "Have you tried to solve this before? What happened?" — Past attempts to solve a problem are the best signal of howimportant the problem actually is. If they haven't tried, it may not be painful enough to warrant a solution.

Current Behavior

  • "Show me how you handle [task] today." — Shadowing or screen-sharing beats verbal description every time. People don't know what they do until they watch themselves do it.
  • "What tools do you use for this? Why those?" — Tool choice reveals priorities and constraints. Someone who cobbled together a spreadsheet solution because nothing else fit is telling you more than someone who listed three SaaS products.
  • "What's the most annoying part of this process?" — "Annoying" is more concrete than "painful" and surfaces the specific friction points that matter day to day.

The Workaround Question

This is the single highest-signal question in discovery: "What have you hacked together to deal with this?"

People don't build workarounds for problems that don't matter. A manual spreadsheet, a convoluted process involving three different apps, a weekly meeting that exists solely to coordinate something that should be automatic — these are all evidence that the problem is real and the current solutions are inadequate. The more elaborate the workaround, the stronger the signal.

Listening for What Isn't Said

The best insights in a discovery interview often come from what the user doesn't say. Watch for:

  • Excited language around workarounds. If someone says "I built this little script that saves me an hour every week" with visible enthusiasm, that script is a product opportunity in disguise.
  • Hesitation when describing current solutions. "Well, it's... fine, I guess" often means the solution is genuinely bad and the user has made peace with it. That's a gap worth exploring.
  • Emotional language around the problem. Frustration, relief, anxiety — these are data. A problem that provokes a real emotional response is more likely to drive behavior change than one that's merely inconvenient.

After the Interview

Don't leave the call with a checklist of feature requests. Leave with:

  • A specific, observed behavior that surprised you
  • A workaround that revealed the depth of the problem
  • A hypothesis about why the current solutions are failing

Then go validate that hypothesis with more interviews — not by asking "am I right?" but by looking for the same patterns in different people's behavior. Patterns across five interviews are a signal. Patterns across twenty are a thesis. Everything else is anecdotal.

The best discovery interview leaves you with more questions than answers. If you walked away certain about what to build, you probably asked the wrong questions.
